title: How to talk to IBS patients about gut-brain therapy
summary: 44% of patients with bowel gut-brain disorders see a CBT referral as a sign they aren't believed. How to frame gut-brain therapy so they follow through.
body_markdown:
Talking to IBS patients about gut-brain therapy is where referrals are won or lost: 44% of people with bowel gut-brain disorders would see a CBT referral as a sign they aren't believed, new data shows.¹ And much of that reaction is shaped before the referral is even written.


Patients aren't closed to the idea, either. In the[same study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12967772/) , 62% of respondents said they'd still try cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) if it were recommended.¹


So the weak link is often the conversation itself: how gut-brain therapy is framed, when it's raised, and who it's offered to. Here's what the evidence shows on each, and the wording that keeps a referral moving.


## Why IBS patients hear a gut-brain therapy referral as "it's all in your head"


IBS patients often hear a gut-brain therapy referral as dismissal because it tends to arrive late, after diet and medication have "failed", and without a mechanism attached.¹


The 2026 data shows how high the perceived stakes are. Compared with controls, adults with bowel disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs) were more likely to compare the risks of CBT to surgery, and less likely to say it carried no major risk.¹


Depression cut both perceived benefit and willingness to try CBT.¹ So the patients who might gain most from specialist care are often the hardest to bring on board.


### Applying this in practice


Lead with the mechanism and the format before you say "psychologist". Patients with bowel DGBIs were 1.7 times more likely than controls to want CBT explained in a single visit with a therapist,¹ so offer the first appointment as one consult to see if it fits, rather than an open-ended course.


For patients with low mood, expect more skepticism and plan a second conversation rather than treating a first "no" as final.


## Which IBS patients benefit from gut-brain therapy? Not only the anxious ones


Gut-brain therapy isn't reserved for IBS patients with psychological comorbidity. In a[trial of 436 patients with refractory IBS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30613000/) , CBT's advantage over education was clearest in those with low or typical anxiety.³


Among patients with low trait anxiety, 71.3% responded to CBT, compared with 34.9% to education. For those with high trait anxiety, response was similar in both arms (60.6% vs 59.2%).³


Real-world referrals look the same. In an[integrated academic service](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4323468/) , referred patients' average depression, anxiety, and somatization scores fell below clinical thresholds. Treatment was split between gut-directed hypnotherapy (48%) and CBT (44%), and averaged just 4 sessions.²


### Applying this in practice


Drop psychological distress as your referral trigger. Persistent symptoms, symptom-focused worry, avoidance (including[fear-driven food restriction](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/low-fodmap-diet-hard-to-follow) ), or poor response to first-line care are stronger cues.


That gives you an honest line for many patients: "I'm not suggesting this because I think you're anxious. It treats how your gut and brain process signals." For patients who catastrophize about their symptoms, our[guide to brief CBT steps in clinic](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/catastrophizing-ibs-cbt-clinicians) covers the next part of the conversation.


## How to frame a gut-brain therapy referral so IBS patients follow through


A gut-brain therapy referral lands best when it's framed as a mechanism-based, time-limited treatment offered alongside medical care, not instead of it.⁵ ⁶


### What to say when you recommend gut-brain therapy


-


**Name the target:** gut-brain therapies act on visceral hypersensitivity and altered gut-brain signaling, the same pathways behind pain, bloating, and urgency.⁵ Try: "The nerves in your gut have become more sensitive, so normal digestion is registering as pain. This treatment works directly on that sensitivity."


-


**Make it finite:** courses are short and structured, often around 4 sessions in integrated care.² Self-guided programs like Nerva follow a 6-week core program, with ongoing maintenance and flare-up support afterward. Try: "It's a short, structured course, usually a handful of sessions with a specialist. If you'd rather do it at home, there's a 6-week program that takes about 15 minutes a day."


-


**Run it in parallel:** the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG)[guideline](https://doi.org/10.14309/ajg.0000000000001036) suggests gut-directed psychotherapy for global IBS symptoms,⁶ and a[Rome Foundation working team](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34529986/) advises that gut-brain therapies don't need to wait for other approaches to fail.⁵ The[new Rome consensus on IBS-like symptoms in IBD remission](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/ibs-like-symptoms-ibd-remission-rome-consensus) makes the same point. Try: "We'll keep going with your medication and diet changes. This runs alongside them, not instead of them."


-


**Use an analogy that fits the mechanism:** diet and medication work at the branches, managing day-to-day symptoms, while gut-brain therapy works at the roots, calming the signaling that keeps them going. Try: "Think of your treatment plan like a tree. Diet and medication work on the branches, the symptoms you feel day to day. This works on the roots, helping your gut become less reactive over time."


> "Brain-gut behavioral therapies have great efficacy. They work really well in placebo-controlled trials. The effectiveness is strong long-term, up to seven years, and they're very safe. Should these therapies be offered earlier? The data suggests yes."
>
>
> – Dr. Jordan Shapiro, Gastroenterologist, The Gentle GI


### Phrases that undercut a gut-brain therapy referral


-


**"We've tried everything else, so let's think about therapy."** This frames gut-brain therapy as a last resort once medical care has failed, when it can start at any point.⁵ Try: "Alongside your medication, I'd like to add a treatment that works on how your gut and brain process signals. It tends to work best when we start it early."


-


**"Your tests are all normal, so it's probably stress."** A normal workup is often heard as "nothing is wrong", and stress becomes the explanation by default. Try: "Your tests rule out inflammation and structural disease. That points to a disorder of gut-brain interaction, where the nerves in your gut have become oversensitive and normal digestion registers as pain."


-


**"I think anxiety is driving your symptoms."** This makes the referral about the patient's mental health, even though benefit from CBT doesn't depend on high anxiety.³ Try: "I'm not suggesting this because I think you're anxious. These therapies help people whether or not they have anxiety."


-


**"I'm going to refer you to a psychologist."** Without context, patients hear a mental health referral. Try: "I'd like you to see a GI psychology specialist. They focus on gut symptoms specifically, using gut-directed hypnotherapy or CBT."


-


**"It might be worth a try."** Hedging signals low expectations, which patients pick up on. Try: "This is a recommended treatment for IBS. The ACG guideline suggests it for global IBS symptoms, and it can sit alongside your diet and medication."⁶

## Why the referral conversation matters more when GI psychology is hard to reach


The referral conversation matters more when GI psychology is hard to reach, because a hesitant patient also faces distance and waitlists. An estimated 46% of US adults live more than 25 miles from a listed in-person GI psychology specialist.⁷


The payoff for getting patients there is real. In the[MANTRA randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32679040/) , 84% of patients in multidisciplinary care reported global symptom improvement, compared with 57% in gastroenterologist-only care. In the patients with IBS, 66% vs 38% achieved a 50-point or greater reduction in IBS-SSS.⁴

Its onboarding explains the gut-brain axis and visceral hypersensitivity in plain English, so it builds on the mechanism you've already introduced. Referrals don't expire, so a patient who needs a second conversation can start when they're ready.

## Frequently asked questions


### Is brain-gut therapy effective for treating IBS?


Brain-gut therapy is effective for IBS, and the ACG guideline suggests gut-directed psychotherapy for global IBS symptoms.⁶ In a[randomized trial of 244 adults with IBS](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/nerva-ibs-rct) , 81% using a digital gut-directed hypnotherapy program improved meaningfully on the IBS Symptom Severity Scale, compared with 63% on an active control.⁸


### Is IBS all in your head?


IBS is not all in a patient's head: it's a disorder of gut-brain interaction, where altered signaling between the gut and nervous system amplifies real physical symptoms.⁵ Many patients have heard the "in your head" line before, so saying this plainly early in care helps build trust.


### Can you do CBT for IBS online?


CBT for IBS can be delivered remotely: in a[network meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2020-321191) , self-administered or minimal-contact CBT was about as efficacious as face-to-face CBT.⁹ Digital gut-brain therapy programs such as Nerva combine CBT-informed education with gut-directed hypnotherapy.

Referrals don't expire, so patients can start when they feel ready.
